Water first. Substrate second. 💧🌱 This is personally my favorite way to add substrate, especially for a no CO₂, no-filter aquarium. I start with about 2 cm of water, then add the substrate directly into it. The water immediately traps most of the fine particles, instead of letting a cloud of dust spread everywhere. I also don’t rinse my substrate, because I prefer to keep everything it contains rather than washing part of the fine material away. Less dust. Less mess. Nothing wasted. An aquarium’s filter does far more than keep the water looking clean. It continuously removes waste, circulates oxygen, and provides a home for beneficial bacteria that break down harmful toxins produced by fish and uneaten food. Without proper filtration, ammonia and other toxic compounds can quickly build up, turning a healthy aquarium into a dangerous environment for its inhabitants. A good filtration system helps maintain water quality, stabilize the ecosystem, and keep fish healthy over the long term. While decorations and lighting may catch the eye, the filter is the unseen engine that keeps the entire aquarium alive.

Tools like siphon vacuums and filtration systems pull out uneaten food, algae, and sediment from the gravel, keeping the environment clean without stressing the fish. What makes this approach effective is balance. Beneficial bacteria remain undisturbed, water chemistry stays stable, and the tank continues to cycle naturally. A quick rinse under the tap will not ruin your beneficial bacteria. The rule about only ever using old tank water is mostly an overstated myth, and both Aquarium Science and large fishrooms like KeepingFishSimple back this up. Tap water contains very low levels of chlorine or chloramine, usually around 0.5 to 2 ppm. Testing shows it takes anywhere from 15 minutes to several hours of continuous exposure to penetrate slimy biofilm and affect nitrifying bacteria. A brief rinse under the tap simply is not enough contact time to do real harm. When a cycle crashes after filter maintenance, it is almost always because an immature filter was scrubbed completely spotless, physically washing the young bacteria away. That happens regardless of whether you use tank water or tap water. Commercial breeders running dozens of tanks rinse sponge filters straight under the tap or garden hose every week without issue, because mature media and tank surfaces like substrate and plants hold plenty of resilient bacteria. For an established tank, a quick rinse in lukewarm tap water is completely fine as long as you never leave the media sitting submerged in untreated water. If your tank is brand new or bare bottom, gently swishing the media in old tank water is still the safer bet while those colonies are young.
